Generally, it is recommended to wait to initiate the 409A process until the debt arrangements and new fundraising are finalized. This strategy ensures that any significant financial changes are accurately reflected in the valuation. However, if you need to issue equity immediately or if those with Non-Qualified Stock Options (NSOs) want to exercise their options now, you can proceed with the 409A valuation request at this moment. Be sure to provide comprehensive details about the tranches and debt arrangements in the "Valuation details" section of the form. Please note, if you do decide to proceed with the 409A valuation now, you may need to initiate another request once all the new fundraising and debt arrangements are finalized to ensure the valuation accurately reflects the most current financial situation. This will need to be discussed with your legal counsel.

When material changes in the business have happened since last valuation, it is recommended to get the 409A valuation updated. Depending on whether the terms for new funding have been discussed/agreed upon, one possible route that could be considered (if options need to be issued now) is to do the new 409A valuation now based on pro-forma cap table (if funding is so imminent; next couple of months and this is known event now). Thanks . Client followed up with the following question: "When doing a 409A for a company does Carta take into consideration the convertible debt? I was able to get a better understanding of how we currently have our 409A done: Here is a summary of the process: The convertible debt valuation process uses a Probability-Weighted Expected Return Method (PWERM) with two main scenarios (Next Equity Financing and IPO) and a sub-scenario within the Next Equity Financing scenario. In the Next Equity Financing scenario, the equity value is projected to the expected financing date. For each simulated equity value, the liquidation preference for the new financing round is calculated. An Options Pricing Model is then used to allocate the simulated equity value (considering convertible debt). If a backsolve for the liquidation preference isn't possible, it's assumed no new financing occurs. In this case, the convertible debt is assumed to convert into preferred shares under the optional conversion after maturity framework, and the equity value is allocated accordingly. In the IPO Scenario, the equity value is projected to the expected IPO date. A Current Share Equivalent (CSE) approach is used to determine the fair value of each equity class, including warrants and convertible debt, which is then discounted. Finally, the overall value is determined by calculating a probability-weighted average of the fair values from both scenarios and then applying a discount for lack of marketability. Does Carta's valuation team provide a similar process? Is there anything more you can provide me about how Carta's valuation team completes their process for companies?"

can you provide some insight here as to whether this mirrors our process or is something we would be able to accomodate?

For the PWERM they're describing, yes it would generally follow the same process if we're factoring in a discrete exit. Not every company has a PWERM though. Its generally for later stage clients who are expecting a realistic exit within 18 months. It would look similar to the following: • Going Concern scenario (Backsolve, GPC, or Income approach or variation of these) that are allocated via an OPM) with a DLOM applied • IPO scenario that is discounted and allocated via CSE, typically also has a DLOM applied that would be different from the going concern. Both post-DLOM values would be weighted to get the final FMV. As for how we would treat convertible debt, we typically default to treating them as standard debt in our walk to equity value, prior to allocating (always for uncapped notes because we dont know what the future valuation would be). If there is a cap, occasionally we'll allocate them in the OPM rather than including them in the walk to equity value, but depending on the cap, it largely offsets either either way.

Hi team! I'm onboarding < and the company is a LLC converting to C-corp in a few weeks. However, they want to request the 409a valuation now. Yes, the valuation of an LLC can differ from that of a C-corp due to structural (cap table) and tax-related differences. Units in an LLC may have different rights than shares in a C-corp. If the company is planning to convert from an LLC to a C-corp soon, doing the valuation before the conversion may require another 409A valuation shortly after the conversion, especially if options are going to be granted based on the C-corp stock. If a conversion is imminent, it's generally better to wait until after conversion for a 409A valuation to ensure it reflects the structure under which equity incentives will be granted. Alternatively, if there’s an urgent need to perform a valuation now (e.g., to grant equity awards beforehand), the valuation firm must carefully consider the conversion and the likely post-conversion structure, and may still recommend updating or redoing the 409A post-conversion. The company should consult with its legal/tax counsel in this regard before making decision.

Hey team! I have an interesting case: this company has a Carta valuation effective on Apr 19, 2024 covering common share classes Common A and Common B. On 6/4/2024, they filed a new COI authorizing only one Common share class. Should they require a new valuation as of 6/4/2024 only for Common? The filing of a new COI and restructuring of common share classes on June 4, 2024 is a material event, and the best practice would be to obtain a new 409A valuation effective on or after that date — specifically tailored to value the new single common class. They should anyways also consult with their legal/tax counsel. One thing to check is also whether they issued options after this material event.
The reason the value of both classes of common is same is because both have the same rights in this situation
If there are no differences between the two share classes (apart from simple things like voting vs non-voting, which we don't consider in the 409A), then the value would be the same.
Its not uncommon that we issue a 409A that only labels one common class value whereas the client has 2 classes of common. The 409A would apply to both.

In this case, since its kind of the reverse, I'd just have them check with their legal counsel. If they're just merging the two classes into one but nothing else has fundamentally changed between the classes (like taking a voting class and non voting class and combining them into a single voting class), and there's no other material events otherwise, their currently active 409A would likely still be valid

Hey , normally we'll look at revenue multiples first. I'd say its our "default". We don't typically rely on it for a first pass (unless it was used historically) as it often leads to more volatile conclusions given the change in either EBITDA or the multiples. If they'd like us to use EBITDA though, then we certain can and theres a number of clients we use EBITDA multiples with. An alternative here that we'll often use is a DCF as well if forecasts are available. We also work with a number of manufacturing companies and each valuation is performed considering whats the most relevant for the target company at the time, be it revenue, EBITDA, DCF, or a combination. As for the industries, this is generally just for the industry overview section. The actual comparable companies we use would be more relevant and we'd work with Management to make sure that the peer set is as accurate as possible. I'd also note that while they might be valued on EBITDA if they're looking for any kind of traditional MA exit, thats for a different purpose than 409A/718 (EG SaaS companies may be valued on ARR but we'll still use a revenue multiple for the 409A report)
since there's also 3921 implications on this as well, I don't think this is a case that our team should handle but I can help with a reply if you'd like.

To the clients point though, for companies that are profitable, I do like to use revenue and EBITDA as a check. If we're using revenue multiples, does the implied EBITDA multiple fall within the range and if so, does it still make sense within the range? (eg is it at the max of the range when the company is ranked near the bottom relative to the peer comps). The Class C shares were issued under a service-based Equity Incentive Plan (structured as Restricted Stock Awards) and were intentionally designed to carry no economic, governance, or participation rights.
